rationale: A wins because it turns the same facts into four real press doors instead of three, and the fourth is not padding: "What it's actually like to rent your running shoes and mail them back to be ground up" is a proper gear/consumer service lane. B has solid bones, especially "On turns running shoes into a subscription you never own," but it leaves the runner experience trapped as proof for another angle and leans the sustainability story toward a gotcha before the facts can carry it. A also names the boring lethal holes: country, price, recycling rate, and a sourced growth claim.
gaps_in_A: The next step says "get answers to the first two questions before drafting anything"; that over-prioritizes sustainability proof when the category, markets, and runner-experience angles also need price, pilot data, and a source.
The markets angle is tagged "funding-mechanics," which is the wrong label for a public-company unit-economics and margin story. The substance is fine; the label wobbles.
gaps_in_B: It never breaks out the runner/service story; it buries the human proof as "one named subscriber or pilot participant" inside the category angle instead of making the consumer experience its own pitch lane.
"putting a core product behind" overstates the update. The facts say Cyclon has a subscription; they do not say On is moving a core product line behind the model.

"the widely-held \"closed loop / fully recyclable\" framing" is decorated inference. On makes a circularity claim, but a missing recycling rate is a verification hole, not proof of a prevailing belief collapsing.
It misses two targeting and fact-check traps A catches: "Nationwide" needs a country, and "one of the fastest-growing athletic brands" needs a source before it goes near a reporter.
